newsitem.title: USA: Floodwaters snarl traffic on Mississippi River.
newsitem.headline: Floodwaters snarl traffic on Mississippi River.

text.p: Millions of gallons of silt-laden water, dumped into the Mississippi by floods in the Ohio Valley, are playing havoc with river traffic in southern Louisiana, authorities said Thursday.
Since Monday afternoon, three separate incidents have closed the river at locations from Baton Rouge down to the Gulf of Mexico, and two riverboat casinos have been forced to shut down.

Traffic on the Mississippi at Baton Rouge has been hampered since a string of 25 barges under tow hit a bridge late Monday. Two rock barges sank, one is missing and another, carrying a volatile mix of gasoline and benzene, capsized.

On Thursday afternoon, authorities still were trying to determine the safest way to offload the capsized barge's cargo, State Police Sgt. Mark Mix told Reuters. Only one-way traffic, one vessel at a time, is allowed there.

Farther downstream near Laplace, about halfway to New Orleans, 12 miles of the river were closed for some 16 hours Thursday as tugs scrambled to return 100 breakaway barges to their moorings, Coast Guard Marine Safety Office Cmdr. Ken Parris said. All the barges, which broke loose about midnight, were repcaptured by midmorning.

At the mouth of the river at Southwest Pass, the only channel for deep-draft vessels to reach the Mississippi from the ocean, a grounded freighter forced the river to close early Thursday morning, Parris said.

He said the Norwegian-flagged Ariel, carrying coal to the United Kingdom, hit a transitory shoal of silt called a "mud lump" and veered onto land. Twelve hours later the ship was refloated and taken upriver to check for damage, he said.

However, the river will remain closed at the pass until the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers completes a survey of the pass depth to determine what draft vessels will be allowed through later Thursday night, Parris said.
The Corps had four dredges operating at Southwest Pass Thursday and two other contracts for dredging are being advertised, Corps spokesman Rob Brown told Reuters.
"It's been a crazy 24 hours," he said. "The situation is extremely fluid, excuse the pun, but we're just trying to stay ahead of the water."
Coast Guard and other officials blamed the traffic snarls, at least in part, on high water on the river which creates additional currents and moves tons of silt downriver from the Midwest.
